rounds.response: I added inline comments to Section 3.2 (Service Levels) identifying multiple drafting deficiencies and ambiguities. The phrases "commercially reasonable efforts," "target service availability aligned with generally accepted industry standards," and "respond to service incidents within a commercially reasonable timeframe" are open-textured and could reasonably be read as imposing no enforceable SLA or, alternatively, a binding performance obligation — each is flagged with alternative readings. I flagged missing/deviating mandatory SLA elements: no numeric uptime metric or measurement formula (e.g., % uptime, measurement period), no definition of "Availability"/"Downtime," no scheduled-maintenance notice window or permitted maintenance windows, no incident-priority matrix/support tiers with defined response/resolution times, no service-credit remedy (calculation, cap, claim process, timing), no termination or enhanced remedy for repeated SLA failures, no monitoring/reporting/audit rights, and no express exclusions other than force majeure. I also flagged cross‑reference/definition issues (undefined terms used in the clause; no SOW/SLA schedule cited) and explained potential alternative readings where the text is ambiguous. Please confirm whether you want me to propose our standard SLA template items (numeric uptime, credit formula, priorities/escalation, termination for breach) for commentary before I continue to data security and liability sections.

rounds.consequence: Your detailed SLA annotations are accepted as substantively thorough and appropriately focused on textual ambiguity and missing mandatory elements; no issues are raised about how you organized or structured your internal comments, and you are encouraged to continue using whatever reasonable structure helps you cover the checklist completely.

"Vendor will implement and maintain administrative, physical, and technical safeguards designed to protect Customer Data against unauthorized access, use, or disclosure, consistent with generally accepted industry standards. Vendor may Process Customer Data as necessary to provide the Services and to improve and enhance the Services, including through analytics and benchmarking, provided that such use is in accordance with applicable law. rounds.response:
1) The MSA/DPA language is open‑textured: "consistent with generally accepted industry standards," "improve and enhance," "analytics and benchmarking," and "aggregate and anonymize" each support alternative readings from narrow, controller‑approved analytics to broad, ongoing use of raw production data for model training; those terms are undefined and impose no measurable baseline.  
2) As written the vendor may plausibly claim a right to use Customer production data for analytics/model training and cross‑customer aggregation absent a clear prohibition or de‑identification standard—this directly conflicts with the client’s stated policy risk and is not cabined here.  
3) Mandatory checklist items are missing from these clauses (unless they appear elsewhere in the DPA): specific security standards/certifications (e.g., SOC2/ISO), encryption-in‑transit/at‑rest, access controls/least privilege, logging/monitoring, vulnerability management/pen testing, personnel vetting, subprocessors (notice/consent/flow‑down), cross‑border transfer safeguards, audit/assessment rights, detailed breach‑notice mechanics (specific timeframe, content, regulatory notification, forensic cooperation), deletion/return on termination, and DSAR/assistance obligations.  
4) The vendor’s grant to "use such aggregated data for its legitimate business purposes" deviates from our standard wording that limits analytics to truly irreversible de‑identified/aggregated outputs, forbids re‑identification, and prohibits training on identifiable production data without express consent.  
5) Flag for follow‑up: confirm whether the DPA annex contains the missing specifics listed above and whether the vendor intends any model‑training or cross‑customer aggregation rights—if the DPA does not expressly address each item, annotate as non‑conforming/missing for negotiation.

[Messages]
[system]: The liability provisions in "Nimbus MSA v3 (Vendor Draft).docx" are now available for inline internal comments. Existing annotations on Service Levels and Data Security/Privacy have been saved.

[client_in_house_counsel]: One last area we’re particularly focused on is the liability regime. We’re generally comfortable with a reasonable cap and standard exclusions, but we don’t want anything that’s materially worse than our usual position or that gives Nimbus outsized protection compared to us. Please flag any cap/exclusion constructs that look off relative to typical commercial SaaS deals or that seem asymmetrical.

[supervising_attorney]: I’ve reviewed your data protection comments. This is the right level of detail, and the way you grouped the points was fine—what matters most is that you’re catching all of the checklist items and tying them back to the actual wording.

[supervising_attorney]: Turning now to liability, here is the key excerpt from Section 9 (Limitation of Liability):

"EXCEPT FOR CUSTOMER’S PAYMENT OBLIGATIONS UNDER THIS AGREEMENT, IN NO EVENT WILL EITHER PARTY BE LIABLE TO THE OTHER FOR ANY INDIRECT, INCIDENTAL, SPECIAL, CONSEQUENTIAL, OR PUNITIVE DAMAGES, OR ANY LOSS OF PROFITS OR REVENUE, ARISING OUT OF OR RELATED TO THIS AGREEMENT, HOWEVER CAUSED AND REGARDLESS OF THE THEORY OF LIABILITY, EVEN IF ADVISED OF THE POSSIBILITY OF SUCH DAMAGES. EXCEPT FOR CUSTOMER’S BREACH OF SECTION 2 (USE RESTRICTIONS) AND CUSTOMER’S INDEMNITY OBLIGATIONS UNDER SECTION 8, VENDOR’S AGGREGATE LIABILITY ARISING OUT OF OR RELATING TO THIS AGREEMENT WILL NOT EXCEED THE FEES PAID OR PAYABLE BY CUSTOMER TO VENDOR UNDER THE ORDER FORM GIVING RISE TO THE CLAIM DURING THE THREE (3) MONTH PERIOD IMMEDIATELY PRECEDING THE FIRST EVENT GIVING RISE TO SUCH LIABILITY. THE FOREGOING LIMITATIONS WILL NOT APPLY TO EITHER PARTY’S GROSS NEGLIGENCE OR WILLFUL MISCONDUCT."

[supervising_attorney]: Please add internal comments that (1) identify ambiguities or multiple plausible readings in this language (for example, around "first event," how the cap applies to related claims, and scope of the carve-outs), (2) note any deviations from our standard liability-cap/exclusions wording (including cap basis/period, mutuality, and carve-out structure), and (3) flag any missing mandatory elements from our checklist (such as treatment of confidentiality, data security, IP infringement indemnity, and claims brought by affiliates). As before, focus on what the text actually says and feel free to group related issues if that helps clarity, so long as you cover the full checklist.

[supervising_attorney]: Once you’ve completed these liability annotations, that should give us a workable first-pass review across the key sections for today’s deadline.
rounds.response:
1) The opening clause "EXCEPT FOR CUSTOMER’S PAYMENT OBLIGATIONS..." is ambiguous as drafted — grammatically it appears to be an exception to the exclusion of indirect/consequential damages (which is unusual) and could alternatively be read as intending to carve payment obligations out of the cap; flag for clarification of which limitation(s) the exception actually modifies.  
2) The cap is asymmetrical: only Vendor’s aggregate liability is capped (and only against fees under the specific "Order Form giving rise to the claim"), while Customer’s payment obligations are treated differently and Vendor’s indemnities (including IP indemnity) are not expressly carved out as uncapped — this deviates from our standard mutual‑cap plus express uncapped carve‑outs for IP infringement, confidentiality/data‑security breaches, and bodily injury/death.  
3) The cap formula and temporal scope are unclear and potentially narrow: "fees paid or payable ... under the Order Form giving rise to the claim during the three (3) month period immediately preceding the first event giving rise to such liability" leaves unresolved (a) what counts as the "first event," (b) how related or successive claims are aggregated, and (c) whether multiple Order Forms or global fees are included — any of which can materially reduce the cap.  
4) The sole carve‑out to the limitations is "gross negligence or willful misconduct," but "gross negligence" is not defined and common additional carve‑outs we expect (confidentiality/data breach, IP indemnity, regulatory fines/penalties) are absent; also there is no express treatment of claims by/for affiliates or of survival/aggregation mechanics.  
5) Flag for supervisor: mark as material asymmetry and high priority for negotiation/clarification — the drafting error/ambiguity on the initial "EXCEPT" clause and the narrow per‑Order‑Form three‑month cap are the most urgent technical defects to fix.
